# Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta (MN 52 (PTS MN i 349))
**ID:** MN 52 (PTS MN i 349)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The eleven doors expounded by Ānanda consist of the four form-sphere jhānas, the four divine abodes (*cattāro brahmavihārā*), and the first three formless attainments, stopping short of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [Hung 2010; Wen 2011; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. In Ānanda's instructions, each attainment serves as an object of insight: the practitioner enters the state and actively reflects that it is conditioned, volitionally produced, impermanent, and subject to cessation [Hung 2010; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Shulman 2014]. Established in that reflection (*tattha*), the meditator either destroys the mental cankers (*āsavakkhaya*) to achieve arahantship or, if any fetters linger, eliminates the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) to become a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) [Hung 2010; Schmithausen 1981; Wen 2011]. In the commentary (*Papañcasūdanī*), Buddhaghosa glosses *tattha* as referring to that unified state of *samatha* and *vipassanā*, emphasizing the integration of concentration and insight into impermanence [Saitanaporn 2009].
The discourse has a direct Pali parallel in AN 11.16 (the *Dasama Sutta*), with closely related treatments of meditative insight appearing in AN 9.36 and MN 64 (*Mahāmālukya Sutta*) [SuttaCentral; Hung 2010; Schmithausen 1981]. Curated non-Pali parallels include two Chinese translations: MĀ 217 in the *Madhyama Āgama* and the individual translation T 92 (*Shizhi jushi bacheng ren jing*), as well as citations in the *Abhidharmasaṅgītiparyāyapāda* (T 1537.15) [SuttaCentral; Schmithausen 1981; Wen 2011]. DharmaNexus detects significant Pali-internal reuse across Anguttara collections—most extensively with the *Ekādasakanipāta* (AN 11) sharing over 32,000 characters—and confirms cross-language alignments with MĀ 217 (T 26, fascicle 60) and T 92, alongside formulaic parallels in Sanskrit texts such as the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* and Tibetan Prajñāpāramitā treatises [DharmaNexus].
